items.html: Stocks had their worst day since April 2025. The S&P fell 4.36%, the Nasdaq 5.52%, the Dow 3.44% and the Russell 4.45%. The Nasdaq is now in a correction, about 11.9% below its record, and the VIX jumped 69.66% to 28.18. All eleven sectors fell, and only about one S&P stock in seven rose. Wednesday's post-election gain on the Dow was gone in one session.

Chips crashed on fears for data-centre growth under a Democratic Congress. Technology fell 8.00% and chip funds fell 11-12%, the worst day for the iShares semiconductor fund since March 2020. AMD fell 17.26%, Micron 17.46%, Broadcom 10.43%, Qualcomm 9.49% after its results and Nvidia 9.26% to 181.60. 5 NovPalantir fell 9.73% to 154.99, with the rest of AI software and hardware.

Neither is exposure. They are worth watching as information about the AI trade and as possible re-entries.

The election turned into a data-centre problem overnight

1. The market re-read the election result. On Wednesday it saw gridlock and bought. On Thursday it focused on what a Democratic Congress and state votes in Texas and Georgia could mean for data-centre buildout, and UBS put about 30% of planned 2028 additions at risk. The companies that sell into that buildout fell 10-20% in a day.

2. It spread well beyond chips. All eleven sectors fell, the Russell fell 4.45% and only about one S&P stock in seven rose. Technology was down 8%, but industrials, which include power and cooling suppliers to data centres, fell 4.12%. The VIX rose almost 70%.

3. The Fed backdrop got easier at the same time. Productivity beat, labour costs fell, and the two-year yield fell about 12bp. December hike odds dropped from above 80% to about two-thirds. That did nothing for stocks on Thursday, but Friday's payrolls now carry more weight for the December decision.

Deal hopes fade a little, and crude bounces

Oil rebounded as the diplomacy looked less certain. Eurasia Group cut its odds of a US-Iran deal and raised its odds of a continued standoff. Tanker attacks continued near the Strait of Hormuz, and Saudi Arabia issued alerts around Yanbu as Houthi attacks went on. Qatar's expected feedback on the talks had not been reported by the close.

The bounce was small next to the fall. WTI settled $90.52, up 2.72%, and Brent $98.29, up 3.88%, against falls of 8.29% and 8.67% on Wednesday. WTI is still about 13% below Friday's $104.12.

For this book the channel is the same. Crude feeds inflation, and inflation feeds the Fed. With oil well off its highs and labour costs falling, the December hike is less certain than it was a week ago.

weekly.headline: A flat book through Alphabet's miss and a chip sell-off that ended October with the Nasdaq down 2.9% in a day
weekly.standfirst: The week's most unusual move was gold, down 2.96%, its second weekly fall, including 3.62% on Friday. The Nasdaq lost 2.0%, the Dow 0.9% and the S&P 0.6%, a third weekly loss, while the Russell gained 1.3%. The week rose on AI funding, with Meta's $95bn equity plan and $63bn for Anthropic's chips, then fell on AI cash flow: Alphabet lost 12.29% after its miss and Intel 28.58% on its guide. The Fed held 10-2 with two votes for a hike, PCE matched forecasts at 3.6% and 3.1% core, and WTI ended at $104.12 after a limpet-mine attack on a tanker. The book held nothing all week. Q4 is +45.38, +2.77R, all realised, with heat at 0R.

sections.html:

A week that looked quiet on the cards and was not quiet at all. Gold fell 2.96% at 1.64σ, after falling 4.14% the week before. Behind it the Nasdaq fell 2.00% at 0.99σ, the Dow 0.85% at 0.89σ, the Russell rose 1.29% at 0.83σ, the S&P fell 0.57% at 0.57σ and WTI rose 0.82% at 0.14σ. Nothing reached two sigma on the week, because the gains of Monday and Tuesday and the losses of Thursday and Friday nearly cancelled.

The indices, precisely. The S&P fell 43.61 points, or 0.6%, to 7,580.07, a third straight weekly loss; the Nasdaq 518.34, or 2.0%, to 25,437.00; the Dow 444.85, or 0.9%, to 51,770.31. Only the Russell rose, 35.94 points or 1.3%, to 2,811.84. For October the Nasdaq fell about 5.3%, its worst month since March 2025, while the Dow rose.

Five sessions, two halves. Monday: the S&P +0.70% and the Nasdaq +0.82% after Meta launched a plan to raise up to $95bn of equity for AI infrastructure. Tuesday: the Nasdaq +1.18% and the Russell +1.16% as banks and Blackstone arranged $63bn for Anthropic to buy Broadcom chips. Wednesday: a calm session into the Fed decision, with crude +2.88%. Thursday: the Nasdaq −1.38% as Alphabet fell 12.29%, with the Russell +1.01%. Friday: the S&P −1.82% at 2.53σ and the Nasdaq −2.86% at 2.30σ, the biggest daily drops since at least mid-September, as Intel fell 28.58% and the chip index 7.20%. The market spent the first half paying for AI funding and the second half marking down AI cash flow.

The bond market rallied through all of it. The ten-year started the week near 5.0%, rose to 5.044% after the Fed on Wednesday, and finished at about 4.94% on Treasury's curve. The two-year ended at 4.56%. December hike odds went from about 83% on Tuesday to above 80% after the Fed and PCE, then eased to about 76% on Friday as stocks fell.

Gold is the reading to explain. In a week with a mine attack on tankers, Hormuz declared closed again and crude at its highest settle in weeks, gold fell 3.62% on Friday alone to $3,875.84 spot, with December futures at a one-year low. It is trading on the Fed, not the Gulf: two officials argued for more hikes on Friday, and a metal with no yield loses most when rates are expected to rise.

No positions all week, and the whole risk budget unused

Nothing in this book traded this week. The last exit was AAPL on 19 October, and PLTR before it on the 15th at 194.25. The book held nothing through Alphabet's 13.6% two-day fall, Amazon's results and Friday's chip sell-off.

Flat was the right place to be this week, but not by design. The exits came on rules and journal calls weeks ago, not on a view of this week. Heat was 0.00R at the start and 0.00R at the end, with the full 3.0R available.

The quarter is +45.38 at +2.77R, all of it realised. Q3 finished at +17.04, +0.84R, so Q4 is already 2.7 times Q3 with two months to run. The week was +0.00. Nothing is open, so nothing in this number moves until a new position is taken.

The market paid for AI funding early in the week and punished AI cash flow late

1. Three hyperscalers reported, and the verdicts followed free cash flow. Microsoft, whose operating cash covered its capex by $18.6bn, beat and ended Thursday nearly flat. Alphabet missed on revenue and EPS for the first time in nearly four years, with free cash flow of minus $9.07bn beside Cloud growth of 103%, and fell 12.29%, its worst day in more than two decades. Amazon grew AWS 39% and set a record margin, but trailing free cash flow was minus $42.4bn; it fell 1.41% on Friday after opening 4.6% lower.

2. On Friday the doubt reached the companies that sell to them. Intel's Q4 guide of $0.25 a share against about $0.43 took it down 28.58%, and the semiconductor index fell 7.20%, with AMD and Qualcomm down more than 10%. Monday's and Tuesday's rallies were about financing: Meta's $95bn equity plan and $63bn for Anthropic's chip purchases. By Friday the question was whether the spending earns its keep, and the answer the market gave was no, not yet.

3. The Fed leaned toward hiking, and the data gave it no reason to stop. The hold at 3.75-4.00% on Wednesday came with two dissents for a hike, from Cook and Hammack. Thursday's September PCE matched forecasts at 3.6% headline and 3.1% core, Q3 GDP grew 3.4%, and Friday's employment cost index rose 3.4% on the year. Then Musalem and Logan argued for more increases, Logan for at least two. Falling stocks moved the December odds only from above 80% to about 76%.

Mines in the strait, Hormuz declared closed again, and talks that never quite start

Crude fell early in the week on diplomacy and rose late on attacks. On Monday and Tuesday WTI fell 3.3% to $99.90 as Qatari mediators and then Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials went to Tehran. On Wednesday it rose 2.88% after the Houthis claimed a strike on Saudi Arabia's largest refinery, which Saudi authorities did not confirm. It eased on Thursday and rose 2.08% to $104.12 on Friday, its highest settle since at least mid-September.

The attacks changed form. On Thursday Iran's navy said a tanker hit a naval mine east of the Strait and caught fire, and an IRGC general said the strait will remain closed until Iran's conditions are met. UK Maritime Trade Operations later said a tanker hit that night had explosives attached to its hull from a small boat, which reports called the first successful attack of that kind in the war. Iran said three tankers hit mines; Oman rescued 25 crew.

The politics are pointed at Tuesday. Trump said Iran had wanted to make a deal but kept dragging it out, said on Friday the war will be wrapped up soon, and has said Washington will not strike before the 3 November midterms. Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Friday, and an Iranian official said Tehran welcomes efforts toward negotiations. Nothing has been signed and nothing has been scheduled. For this book the channel is the same as all month: crude feeds inflation, and inflation keeps the Fed talking about hikes.

For this book the channel is the same. Crude feeds inflation, and inflation feeds the Fed. With oil well off its highs and labour costs falling, the December hike is less certain than it was a week ago.

With nothing open, the question is whether a 4% down day is an opportunity or the start of more. The full 3.0R is available. The VIX at 28.18 means wider daily ranges and wider stops for any new position, so a normal-sized risk buys fewer shares. Payrolls arrive before the open; there is no need to commit before seeing how the market takes them.

weekly.headline: Alphabet's miss took GOOG through its stop, and October ended with the Nasdaq down 2.9% in a day
weekly.standfirst: The week's most unusual move was gold, down 2.96%, its second weekly fall, including 3.62% on Friday. The Nasdaq lost 2.0%, the Dow 0.9% and the S&P 0.6%, a third weekly loss, while the Russell gained 1.3%. The week rose on AI funding, with Meta's $95bn equity plan and $63bn for Anthropic's chips, then fell on AI cash flow: Alphabet lost 12.29% after its miss and Intel 28.58% on its guide. The Fed held 10-2 with two votes for a hike, PCE matched forecasts at 3.6% and 3.1% core, and WTI ended at $104.12 after a limpet-mine attack on a tanker. In the book GOOG gapped through its 305.67 stop at Thursday's open, 283.68, for -42.18 and -2.09R. The week -33.60; Q4 -7.54, all realised, and heat fell from 1.01R to 0.00R.

sections.html:

Gold fell 2.96% for a second week running — the most unusual move on the board, and still under two sigma

A week that looked quiet on the cards and was not quiet at all. Gold fell 2.96% at 1.64σ, after falling 4.14% the week before. Behind it the Nasdaq fell 2.00% at 0.99σ, the Dow 0.85% at 0.89σ, the Russell rose 1.29% at 0.83σ, the S&P fell 0.57% at 0.57σ and WTI rose 0.82% at 0.14σ. Nothing reached two sigma on the week, because the gains of Monday and Tuesday and the losses of Thursday and Friday nearly cancelled.

The indices, precisely. The S&P fell 43.61 points, or 0.6%, to 7,580.07, a third straight weekly loss; the Nasdaq 518.34, or 2.0%, to 25,437.00; the Dow 444.85, or 0.9%, to 51,770.31. Only the Russell rose, 35.94 points or 1.3%, to 2,811.84. For October the Nasdaq fell about 5.3%, its worst month since March 2025, while the Dow rose.

Five sessions, two halves. Monday: the S&P +0.70% and the Nasdaq +0.82% after Meta launched a plan to raise up to $95bn of equity for AI infrastructure. Tuesday: the Nasdaq +1.18% and the Russell +1.16% as banks and Blackstone arranged $63bn for Anthropic to buy Broadcom chips. Wednesday: a calm session into the Fed decision, with crude +2.88%. Thursday: the Nasdaq −1.38% as Alphabet fell 12.29%, with the Russell +1.01%. Friday: the S&P −1.82% at 2.53σ and the Nasdaq −2.86% at 2.30σ, the biggest daily drops since at least mid-September, as Intel fell 28.58% and the chip index 7.20%. The market spent the first half paying for AI funding and the second half marking down AI cash flow.

The bond market rallied through all of it. The ten-year started the week near 5.0%, rose to 5.044% after the Fed on Wednesday, and finished at about 4.94% on Treasury's curve. The two-year ended at 4.56%. December hike odds went from about 83% on Tuesday to above 80% after the Fed and PCE, then eased to about 76% on Friday as stocks fell.

Gold is the reading to explain. In a week with a mine attack on tankers, Hormuz declared closed again and crude at its highest settle in weeks, gold fell 3.62% on Friday alone to $3,875.84 spot, with December futures at a one-year low. It is trading on the Fed, not the Gulf: two officials argued for more hikes on Friday, and a metal with no yield loses most when rates are expected to rise.

GOOG gapped through its stop, and the book ends the week flat

GOOGInternet content · entered 2026-07-27 at 325.86 · exited 2026-10-29 at 283.68 · gapped through the 305.67 stop at the open-2.09R-10.59%-33.60

The week's event in this book was one price: Thursday's open. GOOG started the week at 317.28, rose to 321.89 into Wednesday's results, and opened Thursday at 283.68, 21.99 below the 305.67 stop. A stop cannot fill where a stock never trades, so the exit was the open: -42.18 on the position, -2.09R against 20.19 of initial risk, and -33.60 measured from the week's start. The grid uses the opening print; the actual fill replaces it when it is known.

The gap cost about one extra R, and holding would have cost more. The stop was set to lose about 20.19; the gap made it 42.18. But GOOG closed Thursday at 282.32 and Friday at 278.22, so the open was not the worst exit available. Heat went from 1.01R to 0.00R. This is the second gap through a stop this quarter, after AMZN on 15 October; both were losses that no stop could have capped.

The quarter is -7.54 at -0.39R, all of it realised. Q3 finished at +12.31, +0.58R, so Q4 is 19.85 behind it with two months to run. The week was -33.60. Nothing is open, so nothing in this number moves until a new position is taken.

The market paid for AI funding early in the week and punished AI cash flow late

1. Three hyperscalers reported, and the verdicts followed free cash flow. Microsoft, whose operating cash covered its capex by $18.6bn, beat and ended Thursday nearly flat. Alphabet missed on revenue and EPS for the first time in nearly four years, with free cash flow of minus $9.07bn beside Cloud growth of 103%, and fell 12.29%, its worst day in more than two decades. Amazon grew AWS 39% and set a record margin, but trailing free cash flow was minus $42.4bn; it fell 1.41% on Friday after opening 4.6% lower.

2. On Friday the doubt reached the companies that sell to them. Intel's Q4 guide of $0.25 a share against about $0.43 took it down 28.58%, and the semiconductor index fell 7.20%, with AMD and Qualcomm down more than 10%. Monday's and Tuesday's rallies were about financing: Meta's $95bn equity plan and $63bn for Anthropic's chip purchases. By Friday the question was whether the spending earns its keep, and the answer the market gave was no, not yet.

3. The Fed leaned toward hiking, and the data gave it no reason to stop. The hold at 3.75-4.00% on Wednesday came with two dissents for a hike, from Cook and Hammack. Thursday's September PCE matched forecasts at 3.6% headline and 3.1% core, Q3 GDP grew 3.4%, and Friday's employment cost index rose 3.4% on the year. Then Musalem and Logan argued for more increases, Logan for at least two. Falling stocks moved the December odds only from above 80% to about 76%.

Mines in the strait, Hormuz declared closed again, and talks that never quite start

Crude fell early in the week on diplomacy and rose late on attacks. On Monday and Tuesday WTI fell 3.3% to $99.90 as Qatari mediators and then Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials went to Tehran. On Wednesday it rose 2.88% after the Houthis claimed a strike on Saudi Arabia's largest refinery, which Saudi authorities did not confirm. It eased on Thursday and rose 2.08% to $104.12 on Friday, its highest settle since at least mid-September.

The attacks changed form. On Thursday Iran's navy said a tanker hit a naval mine east of the Strait and caught fire, and an IRGC general said the strait will remain closed until Iran's conditions are met. UK Maritime Trade Operations later said a tanker hit that night had explosives attached to its hull from a small boat, which reports called the first successful attack of that kind in the war. Iran said three tankers hit mines; Oman rescued 25 crew.

The politics are pointed at Tuesday. Trump said Iran had wanted to make a deal but kept dragging it out, said on Friday the war will be wrapped up soon, and has said Washington will not strike before the 3 November midterms. Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Friday, and an Iranian official said Tehran welcomes efforts toward negotiations. Nothing has been signed and nothing has been scheduled. For this book the channel is the same as all month: crude feeds inflation, and inflation keeps the Fed talking about hikes.
